Convert vectors for data preparation

Source: R/type-conversion.R
type_conversion.Rd

Convert text to numbers with destring(), labelled values to labels with decode(), or values to text with tostring(), following Stata's conversion commands. as_numeric() and as_character() are aliases of destring() and decode().

Usage

destring(x, ignore = NULL)

decode(x)

tostring(x)

as_character(x)

as_numeric(x, ignore = NULL)

Arguments

x

A vector or matrix; a vector for tostring().

ignore

NULL (default) or a single string of characters to remove from text before reading numbers, like Stata's ignore(). Each character is removed wherever it appears: ignore = "kg " removes k, g and spaces.

Value

destring() and as_numeric() return a double vector; decode(), as_character(), and tostring() return a character vector. Results have the same length as x; matrices are flattened in column order. Unsupported numeric-conversion inputs, such as lists, raw vectors, and complex vectors, return missing values of the same length. Empty inputs return typed empty vectors. Names, dimensions, labels, and units are dropped, except that tostring() returns character input unchanged, including its attributes. Invalid numeric text adds a problems attribute readable with readr::problems().

Details

Reading numbers

destring() reads text the way Stata's destring does. A value must be a number, optionally with a sign, exponent, currency symbol (dollar, euro, pound, yen), thousands separators (1,234), a trailing percent sign (50% gives 50) and surrounding spaces. Anything else, such as "12abc", "10 kg" or a date, becomes NA with a warning, like Stata's force option; the positions and original values are kept in readr::problems(). Use ignore to remove other characters first, like Stata's ignore(): destring(x, ignore = "kg") reads "10 kg" as 10. Empty strings, "NA" and Stata's "." are missing without a warning; the text "NaN" becomes NaN. Date strings become NA; parse them with as.Date() or lubridate::ymd() instead.

A factor whose levels are all numbers, such as factor(c("1990", "2000")), gives those numbers (1990, 2000). Other factors give their level codes. Labelled numeric variables return their values; labelled text is read from its values like plain text.

Labels, missing values, and units

decode() uses value labels when a labelled vector has a nonempty labels attribute. Without value labels, it uses ordinary character conversion, including for tagged missing values.

destring() and decode() keep SPSS user-missing codes as values or labels. Numeric conversion preserves tagged missing values. Dates become days since 1970-01-01; date-times become seconds since the Unix epoch. Durations and measured vectors retain their numeric values in their existing units. Conversion of large integer64 values to double can lose precision and emits the underlying conversion warning.

Text formatting

tostring() ignores value labels: labelled numeric vectors and factors give their codes. For non-character input, values flagged by is.na(), including NaN, tagged missing values, and SPSS user-missing codes, become NA. Character input is returned unchanged. Numbers are written in full, so 100000 gives "100000", not "1e+05". Dates use as.character(), giving "2024-01-31" rather than day numbers.

The sjlabelled package also exports as_numeric() and as_character(). They differ: sjlabelled's as_numeric() turns non-numeric text into factor codes, and its as_character() gives NA for unlabelled values. Whichever package is attached last masks the other; write tidystata::as_numeric() to be explicit, or use destring() and decode(), which do not clash.

See also

Other conversion functions: na_conversion

Examples

lifeexp |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    region_chr = decode(region),
    region_code = tostring(region),
    region_num = destring(region),
    region_fct = haven::as_factor(region),
    .keep = "used"
  )
#> # A tibble: 68 × 5
#>    region               region_chr       region_code region_num region_fct      
#>    <dbl+lbl>            <chr>            <chr>            <dbl> <fct>           
#>  1 1 [Europe & C. Asia] Europe & C. Asia 1                    1 Europe & C. Asia
#>  2 1 [Europe & C. Asia] Europe & C. Asia 1                    1 Europe & C. Asia
#>  3 1 [Europe & C. Asia] Europe & C. Asia 1                    1 Europe & C. Asia
#>  4 1 [Europe & C. Asia] Europe & C. Asia 1                    1 Europe & C. Asia
#>  5 1 [Europe & C. Asia] Europe & C. Asia 1                    1 Europe & C. Asia
#>  6 1 [Europe & C. Asia] Europe & C. Asia 1                    1 Europe & C. Asia
#>  7 1 [Europe & C. Asia] Europe & C. Asia 1                    1 Europe & C. Asia
#>  8 1 [Europe & C. Asia] Europe & C. Asia 1                    1 Europe & C. Asia
